story-002.text: The yogi Ranum Nuzarget was intently tracing mysterious figures with his cane on the cheerful sand of the summer square garden. An onlooker might have thought that this sad, thin man in a muslin turban was whiling away an idle hour. The matter, however, was more serious. Tracing arabesques whose studied lines, in the very process of their coming into being, helped his strained will to send forth strictly shaped waves of soundless conversation, Ranum Nuzarget, with his strong and cruelly punished soul, was holding passionate discourse with a distant corner of the earth: the abode of the Great Initiation.

story-003.text: An hour passed. Ranum had said everything. Repentance, sorrow, anguish, the horror of being cast out: all this the exile had conveyed to the distant, sultry land, to the Great Initiation. The trembling of the invisible strings that joined him to the omnipresent will of the Highest of the High, of Him whose face he, Ranum Nuzarget, had not been found worthy to behold… that trembling subsided. The strings vanished. Ranum raised his head and began to wait for an answer.

story-004.text: Before him, to and fro, in a motley succession of clothes and faces, passed a multitude of city folk. In this enormous city, seething with a lava of passions (greed, anger, cunning, fear, thousand-hued desires, bewilderment and insolence), Ranum endured the keen torments of a spirit that strives toward the repose of blissful contemplation, yet is compelled to dwell amid the filth, blood and darkness of imperfect beings passing through their lower incarnations. The hell of war and the social earthquake hindered him in performing his inner work. The contagion of the mood of millions, perceptible to any townsman, penetrated Ranum with immeasurably greater force, for the slightest attention of his refined power allowed him to read thoughts; more than that, to know the whole hidden essence of a human personality.

story-005.text: He gazed intently at the passers-by, who now and then glanced curiously at the white robe, the turban and the thin brown face of the Indian, with its motionless black eyes that stayed in the memory like a shout or a blow. So far Ranum had seen nothing out of the ordinary. Beneath a monotonous sameness of outward form there moved a procession of ordinary abominations; but among them, as the term of the awaited answer was running out, there passed someone in no way remarkable to our observation, yet astonishing to Ranum. He was about thirty; he was modestly dressed and healthy, with a pleasant, easy face and a firm step.

story-006.text: Ranum sighed deeply. The passer-by’s soul, perfectly plain to him, was dead, as a clock is dead. Its mechanical functions worked admirably, as was witnessed by the passer-by’s lively, keen glance and by his being overburdened with cares for his family and his bread; but the magical principle of the soul, the divine light of the Great Power, had gone out. A rose that has lost its fragrance might serve as the symbol of this state. The passer-by’s soul had been killed by years of shocks, by the poison of evil impressions. The epoch abounded in them. Their unbroken series, in a crude scheme, may be expressed thus: anguish, oppression, violence, blood, death, corpses, despair. The spirit, shuddering, had glutted itself on them, had grown coarse and died; it had become a corpse to all the agitation of life. Even so a plank flung into a whirlpool of waves, amid the manifold seething of the waters’ forces, invariably keeps the flatness of its surface, moving lifelessly hither and thither.

story-007.text: Ranum had met many such people. Their path demanded resurrection. Meanwhile, having caught the tone of fate with regard to this passer-by, the yogi saw that within two hours at the latest the man dead in spirit would die in body as well. As yet he could not determine what manner of death would make an end of him, but he was filled with great compassion for the unfortunate man. A man who ends his days with a dead soul departs forever from the circle of perfection and of the final attainment of bliss in Nirvana. This man was living through his last incarnation. He was losing everything, without suspecting it.

story-008.text: The passer-by who had so horrified Ranum vanished into the crowd, but the Indian followed his path through the city streets with his inner eye. For the present he left him, listening for the answer of the Great Initiation.

story-009.text: That answer resounded like the rushing of blood, or like the perception of music. It was grim and brief. Ranum heard:

story-010.text: “To him whose name is now Fallen Leaf.

story-011.text: The term of purification is not yet ended.

story-012.text: Ranum! Thou shalt return when thou sufferest no more. Strong is the earthly in thee; destroy it, and awaken.”

story-014.text: Ranum was a victim of the power of imagination. What other pupils of the yogis laboured over for years came to him with great ease. The beginning of training, the starting points for the concentration of inner force, consists in exercises, some of which may be related here.

story-015.text: Seated in a strictly prescribed posture, in surroundings and at an hour determined by an age-old ritual, the pupil imagines a point upon the crown of his head. The image must have the force of reality. The next effort is to transform this point, by imagination, into a glowing coal. Then the coal describes an unbroken circle of fire around the seated man, and the plane of the circle is perpendicular to the earth. Then the circle begins to revolve from right to left with the speed of a spinning top, so that the seated man sees himself enclosed within a fiery sphere.

story-016.text: The average duration of these attainments, each taken separately, is as follows: the point, from one to seven days; the coal, from three months to one year; the circle, from three to five years; the sphere, from five to seven.

story-017.text: An exceptional power of imagination helped Ranum to master this entire series of exercises in less than a year. At thirty he was already preparing to receive the Great Initiation.

story-018.text: Three days before the sacrament was to be performed, he fell: he was crushed by a revolt of fettered young forces, an explosion of desires. All the pure flowers of his spiritual garden were burnt to ashes in an unbridled conflagration. Alone in the desert, in utter solitude, for the final concentration of his highest meditations, he gave himself everything earthly by lightning flashes of an imagination that makes its images material: power, luxury, languor and pleasure. A radiant, many-coloured paradise surrounded him.

story-019.text: When he came to himself, an inexorable command banished him into the world. Here, among the descendants of dark, material life, he was to remain until, amid the gravest trials and temptations, he should become dispassionate and mute to all things earthly. Moreover, on pain of utter destruction, he was forbidden to manifest his power. He was to pass through life as a mere witness of its transient shadows, of its deceptive and motley play.

story-021.text: The grief called forth by the answer passed. Having overcome it, Ranum heard overhead the bright, dense sound of a flying machine. He looked up, where thousands of anxious glances from the crowd were already turned, and, without rising, drew near to the man flying beneath the blue sky at the height of the church.

story-022.text: The bandit was moving with the speed of a gale. Behind his hard, well-fed face, its features tense and swollen with evil will, and behind all his well-developed, healthy body, there flashed the black shadow of murder. He was drunk with air and speed, and his nerves were stirred by the awareness of his perilous solitude above an alien city. He was preparing to drop six bombs with that sense of the terrible, and that rapture before the terrible, which a man feels when the force of hypnosis compels him to hurl himself into an abyss.

story-023.text: The chimney of a six-storey house hid for a minute the white vision drilling the air with its hollow roar, but Ranum, by a secret path of consciousness that we are powerless to comprehend, had already established the connection between the bandit and the passer-by with the dead soul. The man with the dead soul was to perish by a bomb dropped at the corner of Red Street and Black Street. Ranum made himself see him, slowly coming out of a shop towards the tram stop. He saw, too, the empty curve of air, not yet filled by the fall of the bomb, and understood that there was no time to lose.

story-024.text: “Yes,” said Ranum, “he will die without knowing the joy of resurrection. That is the gravest of all villainies conceivable on earth. I will not let it come to pass.”

story-025.text: He knew that he himself would perish, intervening by an immaterial manifestation of will in the material chain of phenomena, but there was not even a shadow of hesitation in his soul. It had been given him to understand what a man loses when he is deprived of the joy of resurrection of a dead soul. Horror shook him. He gathered his will into the effort of a sustained impulse and passed — inwardly — from the bench in the square garden to the white drill of the air, to the man drunk with frenzy, and there barred the way of his spirit with silent commands.

story-026.text: The flying man shuddered; confusion and anguish took hold of him. His limbs seemed to fill with lead; his eyes grew dark. His consciousness became a will-less dream. Not understanding what he was doing or why, he made a series of movements essentially contrary to the aim he had set himself. The machine turned sharply aside, flew out over the river towards a huge empty square and, diving softly downward, was smashed from a deadly height against heaps of cobblestones.

story-027.text: Ranum heard the rumble of harmless explosions and understood that he had committed a crime. Sitting upright, calmly folding his hands, he awaited his execution. At that moment, from the maple that spread its broad, shady branches above his head, a green leaf pecked off by a bird fell onto Ranum’s knees, and Ranum mechanically picked up the tree’s gift in the hour of death.

story-028.text: Then, from the depths of the wondrous spaces of India, out of the air and out of the heart of the Great Initiation, he heard tidings that made him smile:

story-029.text: “Our brother, Fallen Leaf, thou hast committed a great crime!

story-030.text: It is forgiven — for the sake of the sacrifice before which thou didst not halt.

story-031.text: Henceforth, torn away for ever from the holy tree, thou, too unruly to be with us, yet not deserving destruction, for thou didst rise up against the death of the spirit, shalt be solitary and eternally green with living life, like the leaf thou holdest in thy hand.”

story-032.text: Ranum kissed the fragrant little maple leaf and with a light heart left the square garden.
